newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia riot blamed on unnamed groups as toll up.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia riot blamed on unnamed groups as toll up.

text.p: Indonesian Moslem leaders have accused unnamed groups with possible communist links of causing riots in a West Java town this week, where a mob of mainly Moslem youths set buildings and churches ablaze.

On Saturday, hundreds of troops continued to patrol Tasikmalaya, 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Jakarta, after Thursday's violence, apparently sparked by a report of police brutality towards some Moslem teachers.

Hasan Basri, head of the Council of Indonesian Ulemas (Moslem scholars), blamed a "formless organisation" possibly linked to the long-banned Indonesian Communist Party (PKI) for being behind the riot.
"Maybe they are (members of) an amorphous organisation (OTB)," Basri was quoted as saying by the official Antara news agency as saying.
OTB is a government term which refers to unnamed groups suspected of communist-like activities.
Basri said OTBs were always close to any social unrest and quick to take advantage of any situation of potential or actual conflict, particularly in events involving religious believers.

Amien Rais, head of the 20-million-strong Moslem social and educational group Muhammadiyah also was quoted by Antara as saying the crowd in Tasikmalaya was incited after it gathered at the police station to protest at the reports of police brutality.
"I have a strong suspicion that there were people who stirred up the crowd to do the damage. We are not looking for a scapegoat, but it is logical that such a thing can be guessed," he said.

Some normality was returning to the town on Saturday with a number of the shops away from the centre of the damage opening for business as troops continued to block roads and guard the worst hit sections.
"Workers are loading the shells of burnout vehicles onto trucks as others sweep the streets in the centre of town," one witness said.
"Other people, including some religious boarding schools, are painting over the grafitti which says "police are dogs' and "police are traitors'," the witness said.

The military said two people had died in the violence, which focused on businesses owned by ethnic Chinese as well as Christian churches and schools, but a newspaper in the capital Jakarta put the death toll at four.
The daily Suara Pembaruan daily on Saturday said four people had died, including an ethnic Chinese woman who was burnt to death in her shop and a looter who fell off the back of a moving vehicle.
The paper said the bodies of two other victims remained unidentified in a Tasikmalaya hospital. The legal aid institute said 160 people had been arrested, mostly for looting.
Mahmud Farid, one of the teachers beaten by police in Tasikmalaya, said in an interview in the Moslem-orienated daily Republika on Saturday that he condemned the violence.
"Those behind the disturbance were not religious teachers, but people who deliberately wanted to make a riot," he said.
President Suharto, who heads the world's most populous Moslem nation, called in a speech on Friday for unity and religious tolerance.
Suharto noted in his speech that there had been civil and political unrest during the past year.
Twenty-five churches and a temple were burned by Moslems near Surabaya in East Java last October over a case in which a Moslem heretic was subsequently jailed for blasphemy against Islam.
"I believe that most religious people in this country are able to control themselves in facing various religious issues that develop in society," Suharto said.
But he said people should be on their guard against groups in society who could cause trouble among the various religions.
"Religious people should be mature and practise self-restraint, avoiding activities that can create resentment among other people," he said.
While more than 80 percent of Indonesia's nearly 200 million people are Moslems, the state recognises the world's major religions.
